title: Text is not always just text
narration: Hello again, hackers. Last time, we learned that text is not always just text.

title: Bytes can become control
narration: A name can become bytes. Bytes can become numbers. And if those numbers land in the wrong place, they can become control.
footer: control flow leaves its intended route

title: Control is only the beginning
narration: But a basic overflow is only the beginning. It gives us the steering wheel. It does not tell us where to drive.

title: Ret2win has one destination
narration: In a ret2win challenge, the answer is simple. Point the return address at a nice little win function, and the program does the rest for us.

title: Now remove the easy destination
narration: Today, we take away the easy destination. No win function. No friendly flag function. No clean shortcut waiting in the binary.

title: Many imperfect fragments
narration: So instead of returning to one perfect function, we return through many imperfect fragments. Tiny pieces of existing code, chained together by the stack.

title: The stack becomes a program
narration: This is return-oriented programming. ROP. Shellcode brings its own instructions. ROP steals instructions the program already has.

title: ret is just state change
narration: Before ROP makes sense, we need to slow down and look at the smallest moving part: the return instruction.
footer: one instruction · two registers · one stack value

title: A call stores the way back
narration: When a function is called, the CPU stores a return address on the stack. That address means: after this function is done, continue here.

title: ret trusts the stack
narration: When the function finishes, ret does not perform a ceremony. It does not ask whether the address is safe. It reads the top stack value, removes it, and copies it into EIP.
footer: the top stack slot is consumed

title: Valid does not mean intended
narration: That is the whole rule. Ret trusts the stack. If the stack says return to main, it returns to main. If the stack says return somewhere strange, it still obeys.

title: The programmer's story breaks
narration: ROP lives inside that gap. The CPU follows valid rules, but the story those rules create is no longer the programmer's story.
footer: same CPU rules · different control-flow story

title: A tiny bug with no win button
narration: Our challenge is picoCTF two thousand eighteen, can-you-gets-me. It is a good ROP lesson because the source is tiny, but the exploit is not just a single jump.

title: Sixteen bytes and gets
narration: The vulnerable function is almost comically small. A sixteen byte buffer, a prompt, and gets.
footer: input rail has no stop condition

title: gets keeps writing
narration: Gets does not ask how big the destination is. It keeps copying input until the line ends. The buffer can be full, and gets will still keep writing.
items: A A A A A A A A
B B B B  → saved EBP
C C C C  → return address

title: The overflow is the entrance
narration: So yes, there is still a buffer overflow. But in this episode, the overflow is only the entrance. The real topic is what we put after the entrance.

title: Every ret asks what comes next
narration: The first gadget address becomes the fake return address. After that, every ret keeps asking the stack what comes next.

title: The tempting shellcode plan
narration: At this point, the tempting plan is shellcode. Put machine code in the input, jump to the stack, and let the CPU execute our bytes.

title: Data becomes code only with execute
narration: That plan depends on one assumption: the stack must be executable. If the CPU is allowed to fetch instructions from the stack, then data becomes code.
footer: permission decides whether bytes are instructions

title: NX blocks execution from the stack
narration: But this binary has NX enabled. Non executable stack. The input can sit there as data, but the CPU cannot run it from there.
footer: data is allowed · instruction fetch is not

title: Executable memory still exists
narration: So shellcode is blocked, but code execution is not impossible. NX does not say the CPU cannot execute anything. It says this memory region is not executable.
footer: use executable memory · not injected stack bytes

title: Reuse what is already executable
narration: The program's own instructions still live in executable memory. And if we can return into the right tiny instructions, NX has nothing to complain about.
footer: the stack is read · the text segment is executed

title: A tiny job, then back to the script
narration: A gadget is a short sequence of existing instructions that ends in ret. Not because ret is powerful by itself, but because ret gives control back to our stack.

title: pop loads · ret jumps
narration: Take pop EAX ret. Pop EAX reads the next four bytes from the stack and puts them into EAX. Then ret reads the next four bytes and jumps there.

title: Every gadget consumes stack
narration: So every gadget has two effects. The obvious effect is the instruction, like changing EAX. The hidden effect is stack consumption.

title: The stack schedules executable fragments
narration: This is why the stack becomes a program. Not because the stack is executed, but because the stack decides which executable fragment runs next, and what data that fragment receives.

title: Same bytes · different meaning
narration: Instead of writing assembly directly, we write a list of addresses and values. Ret and pop interpret that list for us.
footer: interpretation turns payload into a script

title: ROP is building a CPU state
narration: Now we need the chain to do something useful. For this challenge, the classic goal is to ask Linux to run slash bin slash sh.

title: The syscall ABI is a register contract
narration: On thirty-two bit Linux, a syscall through int zero eighty uses registers as arguments. EAX chooses the syscall. EBX, ECX, and EDX hold the first three arguments.

title: The final state is precise
narration: So our desired final state is precise. EAX must be eleven. EBX must point to the string. ECX and EDX must be null.
footer: each gadget will fill one requirement

title: Construct state without new code
narration: ROP is how we construct that state without writing new code. We need gadgets that load registers, gadgets that write memory, and one final gadget that triggers the syscall.

title: A pointer needs something to point at
narration: The string slash bin slash sh needs to exist somewhere in memory. EBX cannot point to an idea. It needs a real address.

title: Write four bytes at a time
narration: We choose a writable area, like data or BSS. Then the chain writes the string there four bytes at a time.

title: The double slash makes clean chunks
narration: The double slash is not a typo. Slash bin slash slash sh is eight bytes, two clean four-byte chunks, and Linux treats repeated slashes in a path normally.

title: The first write is three steps
narration: The first write is a tiny three-step program. Put slash bin into EAX. Put the writable address into EDX. Then store EAX into memory at EDX.

title: A stack slot can be data
narration: First, ret enters pop EAX ret. Pop consumes the next stack slot. That slot is not an address. It is data for the gadget.
footer: pop interprets the next slot as a value

title: ret selects the next gadget
narration: Then the ret at the end of that gadget reads the next address. That address sends execution to pop EDX ret.
footer: control returns to the stack schedule

title: EDX holds the destination
narration: Pop EDX consumes the writable address. Now EDX is not the string. EDX is the place where the string will be written.
footer: register holds an address · not the bytes

title: mov copies bytes into memory
narration: Finally, mov bracket EDX comma EAX writes the four bytes from EAX into the memory address stored inside EDX.
footer: four bytes cross into writable memory

title: Small boring moves compose
narration: That is the first chunk. Not glamorous, but extremely important. Most real ROP chains are made from small boring moves like this.

title: Repeat for the second chunk
narration: Then we repeat the same pattern for the second chunk. EAX becomes slash slash sh. EDX becomes the writable address plus four.

title: C strings end at zero
narration: And then we write zero after it. C strings do not carry their length around. They end when a zero byte appears.
items: read byte → read byte → read byte
footer: zero marks the end of the path

title: Now the string has an address
narration: Now the string is real. It has an address. EBX can point to it.
footer: an idea became bytes at a location

title: The payload becomes assignments
narration: With the string prepared, the chain changes jobs. It stops writing memory and starts shaping the register state.

title: EAX selects execve
narration: EAX needs the syscall number. So we reuse the same kind of gadget: pop EAX ret, followed by the value zero B.
footer: the same load gadget · a new role

title: EBX must be a pointer
narration: EBX needs the address of the filename string. Not the bytes slash bin slash sh themselves, but the address where we wrote those bytes.
footer: pass the address · not the contents

title: ECX and EDX become null
narration: ECX and EDX represent ARGV and ENVP. For this minimal chain, they can point to zero, or be zero, depending on the gadgets we have.
footer: reuse the zero area after the string

title: A multi-pop gadget has an appetite
narration: Sometimes a useful gadget sets several registers at once. That sounds convenient, but it means the stack must match the gadget's exact appetite.

title: The CPU follows order, not intent
narration: If we accidentally place the EBX value first, it goes into EDX. The CPU will not fix our meaning. It only follows order.

title: Predict the future stack
narration: This is the discipline of ROP. You are not only choosing gadgets. You are predicting how each gadget will consume the future stack.

title: Target state reached
narration: When the setup is finished, the CPU state matches the execve syscall contract.

title: The final gadget uses the state
narration: The final address in the chain points to int zero eighty. This is the moment where the prepared state becomes an operating system request.

title: The kernel decodes the registers
narration: Int zero eighty crosses from user mode into kernel mode. The kernel looks at EAX, sees syscall eleven, and interprets the other registers as execve arguments.
footer: the ABI gives every register a meaning

title: Execute this program
narration: And because EBX points at slash bin slash sh, the request becomes: execute this program.
footer: the pointer resolves into a filename

title: The name was a return schedule
narration: The vulnerable program asked for a name. But the bytes we gave it were not a name. They were a return schedule.
footer: input syntax hid an execution plan

title: ret keeps asking the same question
narration: The stack was never executed. The stack simply kept answering the same question: where should ret go next?

title: NX blocks injection, not reuse
narration: That is the strange power of ROP. NX blocks injected code, but it cannot block the program from executing its own code.

title: One jump versus a chain
narration: This is not ret2win. Ret2win is one fake return address pointing to one useful function.
footer: a single useful function does the work

title: ROP moves the machine by degrees
narration: ROP is many fake return addresses, mixed with values, each one moving the machine a little closer to the target state.

title: Search for states, not a win function
narration: Ret2win asks: where is the useful function. ROP asks: what useful machine states can I assemble from the fragments available.
items: need: load eax → pop eax · ret
need: write memory → mov [edx], eax · ret
state: ROP: which states can I build?

title: The stack describes the future
narration: So the stack stops being a place where functions remember the past, and becomes a place where we describe the future.
items: return to main · return to caller
footer: memory of calls becomes a schedule of actions

title: Humans see intention · CPUs see state
narration: When programmers read code, we see functions, names, intentions, and structure. When the CPU runs code, it sees addresses, bytes, registers, and state transitions.
footer: two descriptions of the same program

title: The machine view is lower level
narration: ROP works because the machine view is lower level than the human story. If a byte sequence is executable and EIP points to it, the CPU will run it.

title: The CPU is obeying perfectly
narration: The CPU is not confused. It is obeying perfectly. The exploit is that we changed the data it obeys.
footer: change the data · preserve the rules

title: Code execution without code injection
narration: That is why ROP is such an important idea. It separates code execution from code injection.
footer: execution and injection are different ideas

title: The whole chain
narration: So, the whole chain is this: overflow to control the first return, use gadgets from executable memory, build the register state, and finish with a syscall.

title: ROP carries order, not instructions
narration: Shellcode says: let me bring my own instructions. ROP says: your binary already has enough instructions. I only need to choose the order.

title: One boring instruction, repeated
narration: And the tiny instruction that makes the whole thing possible is ret. One boring instruction, repeated until the stack becomes a program.

title: Next: ret2libc
narration: Next time, we can go one layer deeper: leaking libc, calculating base addresses, and returning into the shared library every C program carries around.

title: Not code injection · code scheduling
narration: But for today, remember this: ROP is not putting code on the stack. ROP is using the stack to schedule code that already exists.
